title: Constitutional Amendment A: Publication of Proposed Constitutional Amendments

context.text: Referred by the Utah Legislature as H.J.R. 10 (2025 General Session), which passed the House 70-0-5 and the Senate 29-0-0, the two-thirds votes the constitution requires. It takes effect January 1, 2027 if approved by a majority of those voting. A companion statute, H.B. 481 (2025), takes effect if voters approve (per KUER).
Ballotpedia lists two certified statewide measures in Utah for November 3, 2026.

question.text: Shall the Utah Constitution be amended to change how proposed constitutional amendments are published, requiring publication for 60 days immediately before the general election in a manner established by state law instead of in newspapers?

summary.text: Replaces the constitutional requirement that a proposed constitutional amendment be published for two months in at least one newspaper in every county where one is published with publication for 60 calendar days before the general election 'in a manner provided by statute.' The ballot explanation states that, if approved, state statute would require the Lieutenant Governor to publish the full text of all proposed constitutional amendments and other Legislature-referred ballot questions on the Utah Public Notice Website and the Lieutenant Governor's website for 60 days before the election. No fiscal estimate was found.

measure.yesMeans: Changes the constitution so proposed amendments are published for 60 days in a manner set by state law (online, under the companion statute) instead of in newspapers.
measure.noMeans: Keeps the constitutional requirement that proposed amendments be published in newspapers in each county that has one.

argumentsFor.text: Republican Rep. Neil Walter, on PBS Utah's Hinckley Report (as reported by KUER), said newspapers are obsolete and the measure is about modernizing the system: "There has to be a new way to meet the requirement for notice and disclosure to residents," he said. "We're moving online, which is where people are."

argumentsAgainst.text: Mary Weaver Bennett, director of the Leavitt Center for Politics and Public Service at Southern Utah University, disagreed with Walter on the same program, saying (as paraphrased by KUER) that many rural communities still rely on their hometown paper.

researchNotes: The statewide ballot text is taken from the official county ballot published on the Utah Public Notice Website (the same statewide question appears on every county's ballot); the resolution text and legislative votes come from the Legislature's publication of the proposed amendments. The Lieutenant Governor's online voter information pamphlet (vote.utah.gov) carries the sponsors' and opponents' arguments, but the pamphlet PDF available did not include them, so the arguments below come from KUER's report quoting legislators and advocates on each side; they are not the pamphlet's official arguments. Ballotpedia is cited only for the count of certified statewide measures (two). A veto referendum on congressional boundaries, a public-union collective bargaining referendum and several initiatives are tracked by Ballotpedia as not on the ballot. Only one named voice on each side was found in the reporting for Amendment A, so the arguments are limited to those.
